The Primacy of Principle: Why Legal Justice Surpasses Violent Revenge

Introduction

The impulse for revenge is deeply human. When wronged, particularly through violence or severe injustice, the desire to personally inflict suffering on the perpetrator can feel not only natural but morally righteous. Yet this instinct, however understandable, leads us away from justice rather than toward it. Even when confronting a corrupt or inadequate legal system, violent revenge remains morally inferior to legal punishment. This position rests not on blind faith in institutions, but on fundamental ethical principles about human dignity, proportionality, and the kind of society worth building.

The Moral Corruption of the Avenger

The first and most profound problem with violent revenge is what it does to those who enact it. Revenge transforms victims into perpetrators, requiring them to commit acts of violence that compromise their own moral integrity.

When we take justice into our own hands through violence, we assume powers that no individual should rightfully claim: the power to be judge, jury, and executioner. This concentration of roles eliminates the checks and balances that prevent abuse. The avenger operates under the influence of rage, trauma, and personal investment—precisely the conditions under which human judgment is most unreliable. We become what we oppose, using violence to answer violence, thereby perpetuating rather than ending the cycle of harm.

Philosopher Martha Nussbaum argues that revenge is "a defeat for humanity" because it reduces us to our most primitive impulses. By contrast, pursuing justice through established systems—however flawed—requires us to articulate grievances rationally, to appeal to shared principles, and to respect processes larger than ourselves. This restraint is not weakness; it is the exercise of our highest human capacities.

The Problem of Proportionality

Revenge inevitably fails the test of proportionality. Without the deliberative structure of legal proceedings, how does an avenger determine the appropriate response? Pain cannot be precisely measured or equivalently returned. The person who has suffered wrong is the worst-positioned to make calibrated judgments about appropriate punishment.

History and psychology both demonstrate that revenge typically escalates rather than equalizes. Research on vengeance shows that avengers consistently overestimate the suffering they've endured and underestimate the harm they inflict in return. What begins as "evening the score" becomes disproportionate punishment, which the original perpetrator's family or community then views as a new injustice requiring its own response. The blood feud becomes self-sustaining.

Legal systems, even imperfect ones, at least attempt proportionality through established guidelines, precedents, and the deliberation of multiple parties. Sentences can be debated, appealed, and revised. Acts of revenge are final and admit no correction.

The Innocent Victims of Revenge

Violent revenge rarely affects only the intended target. Families are shattered, bystanders are traumatized, and communities are destabilized. Children lose parents; parents lose children. The collateral damage of revenge operations is both inevitable and impossible to justify.

Even when revenge is precisely targeted, it inflicts suffering on those who love the perpetrator—people who may be entirely innocent of wrongdoing. While legal punishment also affects families, it operates under principles that at least acknowledge and attempt to minimize these harms. Revenge recognizes no such constraints.

Furthermore, revenge creates new victims who may themselves seek vengeance, perpetuating cycles of violence that can persist for generations. The Hatfield-McCoy feud, the vendettas of Corsica and Albania, and countless ethnic conflicts demonstrate how revenge transforms isolated wrongs into permanent states of mutual destruction.

Justice Versus Vengeance: A Fundamental Distinction

The purpose of justice differs fundamentally from the purpose of revenge. Justice seeks restoration of social order, protection of the innocent, rehabilitation when possible, and acknowledgment of wrongdoing according to shared principles. Revenge seeks satisfaction of personal grievance and the infliction of suffering.

Justice is theoretically impartial; it applies the same standards regardless of who commits the offense. Revenge is inherently partial, applying only to those who have wronged us personally. Justice can be critiqued and reformed because it appeals to public standards. Revenge answers only to private feelings.

This distinction matters because it determines whether we build societies based on principles or power. A society that endorses revenge as legitimate is one where might makes right and where the vulnerable have no protection except what they can personally enforce. Such societies inevitably favor the strong over the weak, the violent over the peaceful.

The Challenge of Corrupt Systems

The strongest objection to this argument addresses corruption: What when legal systems themselves are unjust? When courts serve the powerful, when police are complicit in crimes, when laws protect perpetrators rather than victims, doesn't revenge become not merely justified but necessary?

This objection deserves serious engagement, for corrupt legal systems are not theoretical abstractions but lived realities for millions. Yet even here, violent revenge remains the inferior option for several reasons.

First, revenge doesn't reform systems. Attacking individual perpetrators does nothing to address the institutional corruption that enabled them. The corrupt system continues operating, producing new victims and new perpetrators. Revenge offers the illusion of justice without its substance.

Second, revenge often strengthens corrupt systems. Authorities in corrupt systems frequently welcome opportunities to portray reformers or victims as violent criminals, using such acts to justify further repression. Extra-legal violence, even when morally motivated, provides cover for those who benefit from lawlessness.

Third, alternatives exist. Even in deeply corrupt environments, history shows that organized reform movements, international pressure, documentation and exposure of abuses, and appeals to higher courts or alternative jurisdictions can achieve change that revenge cannot. These approaches are neither easy nor quick, but they build rather than destroy possibilities for genuine justice.

The civil rights movement in the United States faced a profoundly corrupt legal system in which the law itself was unjust and law enforcement was complicit in terrorism. Yet leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. understood that violent revenge would destroy both the moral authority of the movement and its practical prospects for success. By insisting on nonviolent resistance and appeals to legal and constitutional principles, the movement exposed the system's corruption while building a better alternative.

Similarly, post-apartheid South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission chose restorative justice over revenge despite decades of brutal oppression. While imperfect, this approach broke cycles of violence that revenge would have perpetuated indefinitely.

The Slippery Slope of Extra-Legal Violence

Accepting revenge as legitimate in corrupt systems creates impossible line-drawing problems. Who determines which systems are corrupt enough to justify revenge? Which wrongs are severe enough? Who counts as a legitimate target? Once we accept that individuals may use violence based on their own assessment of justice, we abandon any shared standard whatsoever.

This doesn't mean corrupt systems deserve respect or obedience. Civil disobedience, resistance, and revolution may all be justifiable. But these are not equivalent to revenge. Revolution seeks systemic change through force when peaceful means are exhausted; revenge seeks personal satisfaction through violence against individuals.

Even revolution, when justified, must be constrained by ethical principles and the goal of establishing legitimate legal systems—not by personal vengeance. Movements that lose sight of this distinction often replace one tyranny with another, as perpetrators of revenge become the new oppressors.

The Virtue of Restraint

There is profound moral strength in restraint—in refusing to exercise violence even when we have the capacity and justification to do so. This restraint demonstrates commitment to principles above personal satisfaction. It shows respect for human dignity even in those who have violated it. It maintains the moral distinction between victim and perpetrator.

Viktor Frankl, the Holocaust survivor and psychiatrist, wrote powerfully about the prisoners who shared their last piece of bread or offered comfort to others in concentration camps—the most corrupt and unjust environment imaginable. Their restraint and humanity in circumstances that might have justified any revenge demonstrated what he called "the last of human freedoms": the freedom to choose one's response to circumstances.

Choosing not to seek violent revenge when wronged is an exercise of that freedom. It is a declaration that we are more than our wounds, more than our rage, more than the wrongs done to us.

Building the World We Want

Ultimately, the case against revenge rests on a vision of the society we wish to create. Every act of revenge declares that personal judgment and force should trump shared institutions and principles. Every restraint in favor of legal processes, however imperfect, reinforces the possibility of a society governed by law rather than violence.

This is not naive idealism. It is a pragmatic recognition that the alternatives to legal systems—vigilantism, blood feuds, and the rule of the strong—produce vastly more suffering than even deeply flawed institutions. It is also a moral recognition that the means we use shape the ends we achieve. Societies built on revenge become societies of perpetual violence; societies that insist on legal processes, accountability, and reform maintain the possibility of genuine justice.

Conclusion

The argument against violent revenge does not require us to believe legal systems are perfect, or even adequate. It requires only that we recognize revenge as worse—worse in its effects on those who practice it, worse in its disregard for proportionality and due process, worse in its creation of new victims, worse in its perpetuation of cycles of violence, and worse in its destruction of possibilities for genuine justice.

When legal systems fail us, the answer is not to abandon the aspiration for justice but to fight for better systems. This fight requires courage, persistence, and often sacrifice. It lacks the immediate satisfaction of revenge. But it alone offers hope for justice that is more than the temporary triumph of one party's violence over another.

In choosing legal justice over violent revenge—even when that choice is difficult, even when systems are corrupt—we affirm our commitment to universal principles over particular grievances, to human dignity over the infliction of suffering, and to the painstaking work of building just institutions over the momentary satisfaction of destruction. This is not weakness but wisdom, not surrender but the truest form of moral victory.

The Moral Imperative of Legal Punishment Over Violent Revenge

An Argument for Institutional Justice, Even in Imperfect Systems

Throughout human history, the tension between personal vengeance and institutional justice has shaped civilizations, toppled governments, and defined moral philosophy. When legal systems fail — when corruption seeps into courtrooms, when the powerful escape accountability, and when the victimized are left without recourse — the temptation to embrace violent revenge becomes viscerally understandable. Yet even in the shadow of a corrupt legal system, violent revenge remains morally inferior to legal punishment. This essay argues that the ethical, philosophical, and practical foundations of this position are not only defensible but essential to the preservation of human dignity, social order, and genuine justice.

I. The Distinction Between Justice and Vengeance

At the heart of this debate lies a fundamental conceptual distinction that must not be collapsed: the difference between justice and vengeance. Justice, even in its most imperfect institutional forms, aspires to impartiality, proportionality, and the restoration of moral balance within a community. Vengeance, by contrast, is inherently personal, driven by emotion, and oriented toward the satisfaction of the aggrieved individual rather than the healing of a broader social fabric.

The philosopher Robert Nozick drew a critical distinction between the two concepts. Retribution, he argued, is governed by a principle of proportionality — the punishment must fit the crime. Revenge, however, knows no such limit. The person seeking revenge determines the severity of the response based on their own emotional state, their subjective perception of the harm suffered, and their desire to see the offender suffer. There is no external check, no dispassionate evaluation, no requirement of evidence or due process. The avenger is simultaneously the victim, the judge, the jury, and the executioner.

This concentration of roles in a single individual is not merely procedurally problematic — it is morally dangerous. Human beings, when driven by grief, rage, or a sense of betrayal, are notoriously poor judges of proportionality. A father who loses a child to a drunk driver may feel that no punishment is severe enough. A community wronged by a corrupt official may demand blood when justice would call for removal from office and imprisonment. The very emotions that make the desire for revenge comprehensible are the same emotions that make revenge unreliable as a mechanism of justice.

Even when the legal system is corrupt, it retains a structural aspiration toward these ideals. A corrupt court may fail to deliver justice, but the framework of legal punishment — with its emphasis on evidence, proportionality, and procedural fairness — remains morally superior to the unchecked authority of the individual avenger. The corruption of a system does not invalidate the principles upon which it was built; rather, it calls for reform, resistance, and renewal of those principles.

II. The Moral Autonomy Argument

Immanuel Kant's moral philosophy provides one of the most powerful arguments against violent revenge. For Kant, moral actions must be governed by universalizable principles — maxims that one could will to become universal laws without contradiction. The question, then, is whether one could universalize the principle of violent revenge.

If every person who believed themselves to be a victim of injustice were entitled to exact violent revenge, the result would be moral chaos. Each individual's sense of grievance would become sufficient justification for violence, and there would be no objective standard by which to evaluate competing claims. The murder victim's family claims the right to kill the murderer. The murderer's family, believing the killing was justified, claims the right to avenge their fallen relative. The cycle perpetuates itself indefinitely, with each act of revenge generating a new grievance and a new justification for violence.

This is not a hypothetical scenario. The history of blood feuds — from the Hatfields and McCoys in Appalachian America to the centuries-long vendettas in Corsica, Albania, and the Scottish Highlands — demonstrates the devastating consequences of cultures that accept violent revenge as a legitimate response to injustice. These feuds consumed entire communities, destroyed families across generations, and created cycles of violence that could only be broken by the imposition of external legal authority or the exhaustion of the warring parties.

Kant would argue that violent revenge treats the avenger's subjective sense of justice as an absolute moral authority, which is a form of moral arrogance incompatible with the equal dignity of all rational beings. Legal punishment, even when administered imperfectly, at least aspires to treat all individuals according to the same standards and to subject claims of justice to external evaluation. The avenger, by taking justice into their own hands, implicitly asserts that their moral judgment is superior to any collective determination — a claim that, if universalized, would undermine the very possibility of a moral community.

III. The Problem of Epistemic Limitations

One of the most compelling moral arguments against violent revenge concerns the problem of knowledge. Legal systems, for all their flaws, are designed to gather evidence, hear testimony, consider multiple perspectives, and arrive at determinations of guilt through structured deliberation. The individual avenger enjoys no such epistemic resources.

Consider the frequency with which initial perceptions of guilt prove to be wrong. The Innocence Project has documented hundreds of cases in which individuals were convicted of serious crimes — sometimes spending decades in prison — only to be exonerated by DNA evidence or other new information. If the formal legal system, with its investigators, attorneys, forensic experts, and appellate courts, can make such grave errors, how much more likely is it that an individual acting on personal conviction and emotional impulse will punish the wrong person?

The history of lynching in the American South provides a harrowing illustration of this danger. Mobs that believed themselves to be instruments of justice — responding to alleged crimes that the legal system had failed to address — tortured and murdered thousands of people, many of whom were entirely innocent of the accusations against them. The "justice" of the mob was indistinguishable from racial terrorism, and the emotional certainty of the participants was no guarantee of moral rightness.

Even in cases where the identity of the wrongdoer is not in question, the avenger's understanding of the circumstances may be incomplete. Legal systems are designed to consider mitigating factors, extenuating circumstances, and the mental state of the accused. The avenger, consumed by rage and grief, is unlikely to engage in such nuanced evaluation. The result is a form of "justice" that is blind not in the admirable sense of impartiality, but in the dangerous sense of willful ignorance.

This epistemic humility — the recognition that our individual understanding of events is limited and potentially distorted — is one of the strongest moral reasons to prefer institutional mechanisms of justice, even imperfect ones, over personal violence. To act with violent finality on the basis of incomplete knowledge is to risk committing an injustice at least as grave as the one that provoked the desire for revenge.

IV. The Corruption Objection and Its Limitations

The strongest argument in favor of violent revenge is the corruption objection: when the legal system is so thoroughly corrupt that it cannot deliver justice, individuals are morally entitled — perhaps even morally obligated — to take justice into their own hands. This argument has intuitive force. Surely, one might argue, a victim of state-sponsored violence who cannot seek redress through state institutions is justified in seeking violent retribution against their oppressors.

This objection deserves serious engagement, but it ultimately fails to establish that violent revenge is more just than legal punishment. Several considerations undermine the corruption objection.

First, the corruption of a legal system exists on a spectrum. Very few legal systems are so thoroughly corrupt that they deliver no justice whatsoever. Even in deeply flawed systems, some cases are resolved fairly, some judges act with integrity, and some mechanisms for accountability function as intended. The appropriate response to partial corruption is reform — not the abandonment of legal mechanisms in favor of personal violence. To reject the entire edifice of legal justice because of its imperfections is to commit the fallacy of the perfect being the enemy of the good.

Second, the corruption objection proves too much. If the corruption of legal institutions justifies violent revenge, then it justifies violent revenge by anyone who perceives the system as corrupt — including those whose grievances are illegitimate, those whose perception of corruption is mistaken, and those who would use the language of justice to pursue purely selfish ends. The argument provides no principled way to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate acts of revenge, because it removes the very institutional mechanisms that are designed to make such distinctions.

Third, and most importantly, the corruption objection conflates two different moral questions: whether the legal system is delivering justice, and whether violent revenge constitutes justice. The failure of the legal system does not, by itself, transform revenge into justice. A corrupt legal system is unjust; violent revenge is also unjust, but for different reasons. The moral deficiencies of one do not cure the moral deficiencies of the other. The victim of a corrupt system who takes violent revenge has not achieved justice — they have merely added another injustice to the ledger.

This is a crucial point that advocates of revenge often overlook. The moral case against violent revenge does not depend on the assumption that legal systems are perfect or even adequate. It depends on the recognition that violent revenge possesses its own inherent moral deficiencies — its lack of proportionality, its epistemic limitations, its tendency to escalate, and its incompatibility with universalizable moral principles — that are not remedied by the failures of the alternative.

V. The Consequentialist Case

Even setting aside deontological moral concerns, the consequentialist case against violent revenge is overwhelming. Societies that tolerate or encourage violent revenge consistently demonstrate worse outcomes on virtually every measure of human wellbeing than societies that channel the desire for justice through institutional mechanisms.

The cycle of violence that revenge engenders is perhaps the most obvious consequentialist concern. Violence begets violence. The victim who becomes an avenger creates new victims, who in turn may seek their own revenge. This cycle, once initiated, is extraordinarily difficult to break. The history of ethnic and sectarian conflicts — in the Balkans, in Rwanda, in Northern Ireland, in the Middle East — demonstrates that cultures of revenge can sustain violence across centuries, consuming countless innocent lives in the process.

Moreover, the normalization of violent revenge erodes the social trust and institutional legitimacy that are prerequisites for the development of just legal systems. If citizens believe that justice is best served through personal violence rather than institutional mechanisms, they have no incentive to invest in improving those mechanisms. The result is a self-fulfilling prophecy: the legal system remains corrupt because citizens have abandoned it, and citizens continue to resort to violence because the legal system remains corrupt.

By contrast, societies that have made the collective decision to channel the desire for justice through legal institutions — however imperfect — have generally experienced declining rates of violence, increasing social trust, and gradual improvement in the fairness and effectiveness of their legal systems. The legal systems of Scandinavia, for example, did not emerge fully formed as models of justice. They developed over centuries through a process of reform, contestation, and gradual improvement that was only possible because the societies in question had rejected violent revenge as a legitimate alternative.

The philosopher Steven Pinker has documented the dramatic decline in violence that has accompanied the development of state institutions, including legal systems, over the course of human history. While these institutions have often been unjust, their very existence has created the conditions for moral progress by establishing a framework within which concepts of rights, due process, and equal treatment could develop and be progressively realized.

VI. The Virtue Ethics Perspective

From the perspective of virtue ethics, violent revenge is corrosive to the moral character of the avenger. Aristotle argued that virtue consists in the cultivation of dispositions that enable human flourishing — dispositions like courage, temperance, justice, and practical wisdom. Violent revenge cultivates none of these virtues and undermines several of them.

The person who takes violent revenge may believe they are exercising courage, but true courage, as Aristotle understood it, involves facing danger for the right reasons and in the right measure. Revenge is typically motivated not by a courageous commitment to justice but by rage, humiliation, and the desire to reassert dominance. It requires not the disciplined courage of the just warrior but the reckless abandon of the person who has subordinated reason to passion.

Temperance — the capacity to moderate one's desires and emotions — is perhaps the virtue most directly undermined by violent revenge. The avenger has, by definition, surrendered to the most extreme of emotional impulses. Rather than processing grief and anger through reflection, community, and constructive action, the avenger allows these emotions to dictate their behavior, often with catastrophic consequences for themselves and others.

Most significantly, violent revenge undermines the virtue of justice itself. True justice, in the Aristotelian sense, involves giving each person their due — not as determined by the subjective judgment of a single aggrieved individual, but as determined by a community of rational beings deliberating together about the common good. The avenger's "justice" is a counterfeit that substitutes personal satisfaction for genuine moral order.

The effect of revenge on the avenger's character is also worth considering. Numerous psychological studies have shown that acts of revenge, rather than providing the satisfaction and closure that avengers anticipate, tend to intensify negative emotions and prolong psychological suffering. The person who takes revenge is more likely to ruminate on their grievance, not less. They are more likely to experience guilt, anxiety, and moral distress. The act of violence, rather than restoring the avenger's sense of moral order, creates a new source of moral disorder within their own psyche.

VII. Revenge and the Corruption of Moral Language

One of the subtlest dangers of violent revenge is its capacity to corrupt moral language. When we describe an act of violent revenge as "justice," we degrade the concept of justice itself. Justice becomes merely another name for the satisfaction of the powerful, the ruthless, or the most aggrieved. The careful distinctions between justice and vengeance, between punishment and cruelty, between accountability and domination, are erased.

This corruption of moral language has real consequences. When societies accept the equation of revenge with justice, they lose the conceptual resources necessary to critique their own practices. If justice is simply what the aggrieved party determines it to be, then there is no standpoint from which to argue that a particular act of "justice" is disproportionate, misdirected, or cruel. The moral vocabulary necessary for reform — for the identification and correction of injustice — is gutted.

Consider the language of "honor killings" in certain cultural contexts. These acts of extreme violence are described by their perpetrators as acts of justice — the restoration of family honor in response to a perceived transgression. But the equation of murder with justice in these cases is precisely what makes critique so difficult within the cultural frameworks that accept it. By preserving the distinction between justice and revenge, between legal punishment and personal violence, we preserve the moral language necessary to identify and challenge injustice wherever it occurs.

VIII. The Path Forward: Reform, Not Revenge

If violent revenge is not the answer to a corrupt legal system, what is? The history of moral and political progress suggests several alternatives, all of which are morally superior to personal violence.

Civil disobedience, as practiced by Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., represents one powerful response to institutional injustice. By refusing to comply with unjust laws while accepting the legal consequences of that refusal, practitioners of civil disobedience expose the corruption of the system without adding to the sum of violence in the world. Their moral authority derives precisely from their refusal to resort to the methods of their oppressors.

Restorative justice offers another alternative. Rather than focusing on punishment — whether legal or extralegal — restorative justice seeks to repair the harm caused by wrongdoing through dialogue, reconciliation, and community engagement. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission in post-apartheid South Africa represents perhaps the most ambitious experiment in restorative justice in human history. Rather than pursuing violent revenge against the architects and agents of apartheid, South African society chose a process of testimony, acknowledgment, and conditional amnesty that, while deeply imperfect, avoided the catastrophic violence that many observers had predicted and created a foundation for a new democratic order.

Institutional reform, pursued through political organizing, advocacy, litigation, and democratic participation, represents the most durable response to corruption. Legal systems are not static; they are shaped by the values, priorities, and efforts of the societies they serve. The Harder Road: Why Justice Must Never Wear the Mask of Vengeance

I. The Seduction of Revenge

Let's be honest about what revenge offers us. It offers certainty. It offers speed. It offers the visceral, burning satisfaction of knowing that someone who caused suffering has now received suffering in return. It whispers to us in our darkest moments: "You know who did this. You know what they deserve. Why wait? Why trust a broken system when you can deliver what is owed — right here, right now?"

That voice is powerful. It is ancient. It is human.

But it is not the voice of justice. It is the voice of pain wearing justice's clothing.

It requires that the person least capable of impartiality be given absolute power over another human being's fate.

We would never accept this in any other domain of life. We don't let surgeons operate on their own children — not because they lack skill, but because love clouds judgment. We don't let athletes referee their own games. We understand, in every other context, that emotional involvement distorts perception.

Yet somehow, when it comes to the gravest power one person can exercise over another — the power to harm, to maim, to kill — we entertain the fantasy that rage produces righteousness.

It does not. It never has. It never will.

Our stories are full of noble avengers. Cinema glorifies them. Literature celebrates them. We watch a father hunt down his daughter's killers and we cheer. We see a wronged hero take the law into their own hands and we feel something deep within us satisfied.

But stories are not reality. Stories have screenwriters who ensure the hero targets the right person. In real life, there is no screenwriter. In real life, the avenger can be wrong.

And history tells us — with a mountain of evidence so high it blocks out the sun — that avengers are wrong with terrifying frequency.

Lynchings in the American South were acts of revenge. They were carried out by people who believed — with absolute, unshakeable conviction — that they were delivering justice against the guilty. They were wrong. They were catastrophically, unforgivably wrong. And the people who swung from those trees had no appeal, no defense, no voice.

Blood feuds that have consumed families and communities for generations — in Albania, in Sicily, in Appalachia, in countless places across this world — began with a single act of "justified" revenge. The principle of legal punishment says: No one should be harmed without evidence, without a hearing, without the opportunity to defend themselves, and without a standard that exists beyond the emotions of the moment.

You will want a defense. You will want every protection that the principle of legal justice provides.

Revenge is only appealing when you imagine yourself as the one delivering it. The moment you imagine yourself on the receiving end — wrongly — the entire edifice collapses.

I want to close with this.

Choosing legal justice over revenge is not weakness. It is not passivity. It is not indifference to suffering.

It is, in fact, the harder choice. It is the choice that requires you to restrain your most powerful impulses in service of a greater good. It is the choice that requires you to trust in something larger than your own pain. It is the choice that demands you remain committed to a principle even when — especially when — that principle has not yet been fully realized.

Was it easy? No. Was it satisfying in the way revenge might have been? No. Was it right? Absolutely. Unequivocally. For all time.

The path of justice is long. It is winding. It is frustrating beyond measure. There will be days when the system fails so spectacularly that revenge seems not just tempting but logical.

On those days, I ask you to remember: justice is not a feeling. It is not the hot satisfaction of watching your enemy suffer. Justice is a commitment — a commitment to the radical, difficult, beautiful idea that every human being, no matter what they have done, is entitled to a process before they are punished. That no one — no one — should have the unchecked power to be judge, jury, and executioner.

When we abandon that commitment, we do not become heroes. We become the very thing we claim to be fighting against: people who inflict suffering based on nothing more than their own conviction that they are right.

Hold the system accountable. Demand reform. Fight corruption with every ounce of your strength. Tear down unjust institutions and build better ones in their place.

But do not pick up the sword of revenge and call it justice.

Because it is not justice. It has never been justice. And as long as we have the courage to insist on something better, it never will be.
